explain.say: A smell is made of tiny molecules floating in the air. Freshly baked bread or a flower gives off molecules that spread out until some reach your nose.

explain.say: The molecules spread by diffusion, drifting and bumping through the air from where they are crowded to where they are scarce, which is why a smell fills a room.
High in your nose is a patch of smell cells covered in mucus. Molecules dissolve in it and fit onto receptors. Humans have about 400 kinds, and each smell switches on its own pattern of them.

faq.q: What is a smell made of?
faq.a: A smell is made of molecules that escape from a substance into the air. Your nose detects these molecules; things that give off no molecules into the air, like a stone, have almost no smell.
asks: Why do some things have no smell?

faq.q: How does the nose tell different smells apart?
faq.a: Humans have about 400 types of smell receptor. Each smell molecule switches on a different combination of them, like a code, and the brain learns to recognise each pattern.
asks: How many smells can we detect?

faq.q: Why do smells bring back memories?
faq.a: Smell signals go to the olfactory bulb, which links directly to brain areas for memory and emotion, the hippocampus and amygdala. So a smell can recall a place or feeling very strongly.
asks: Why does a smell remind me of my grandma?

faq.q: Why do I stop noticing a smell after a while?
faq.a: Smell cells adapt: if a smell stays the same, they send fewer signals and the brain stops paying attention. This lets you notice new smells, which may be more important.
asks: Why can't I smell my own house?

faq.q: Why do dogs smell so much better than people?
faq.a: Dogs have far more smell cells and a much larger part of the brain for handling smells, plus a nose shape that keeps sniffed air over the smell patch. They can detect some smells at far lower amounts than we can.
asks: How good is a dog's nose?
Do animals smell better than us?

facts: Humans have about 400 working types of smell receptor.
Smell signals reach brain areas for memory and emotion more directly than signals from the other senses.
